title: One road or three?
hook: One road goes straight to G. Three cheap ones go the long way. Which route wins?

knows: spreading out from a start finds the fewest steps (wave-from-the-corner)
doesNotKnow: that with costs on roads the fewest-road route can be the dearest, and how settling the smallest label finds true costs

misconception: The route with the fewest stops is the cheapest.
objective: The learner can settle S, A, B, G in order of smallest label, watch G's label drop from 10 to 6, and explain why settling the smallest label first gives true cheapest costs when no cost is negative.

claims.text: With roads S–G 10, S–A 2, A–B 2 and B–G 2, the cheapest cost from S to G is 2 + 2 + 2 = 6, and the one-road route costs 10.
claims.source: Demo.tsx runAll(): final labels S 0, A 2, B 4, G 6. Builder re-ran the relaxation in Node: same.

claims.text: Settling S gives A 2 and G 10; settling A gives B 4; settling B drops G from 10 to 6.
claims.source: Demo.tsx settle() trace on the QA path (S, A, B, G); messages show each update.

claims.text: Settling the smallest label first is safe: with no negative costs, a route found later can only cost more, so each settled label is a true cheapest cost.
claims.source: CLRS (3rd ed.) 24.3, Theorem 24.6 (correctness of Dijkstra's algorithm for non-negative weights). It can fail with negative weights (CLRS 24.3 discussion); not shown on stage.
E. W. Dijkstra, 'A note on two problems in connexion with graphs', Numerische Mathematik 1, 269-271, 1959.

claims.text: A label is the cheapest cost from S found so far.
claims.source: Definition of the tentative distance d[v] (CLRS 24.1, 'shortest-path estimate').

recall.question: Roads: P–Q costs 7. P–R costs 3 and R–Q costs 3. Settling the smallest label first, what is Q's final label?
recall.why: Settling P gives R 3 and Q 7; settling R (the smaller) drops Q to 3 + 3 = 6, cheaper than the one-road 7.
